correctness.rationale: The surviving pairs are precisely those selecting different blocks of the partition into erased pairs and residual singletons. There are at least three blocks, and the class-total hypersimplex decomposition followed by selecting coordinates in each chosen class proves the claimed hull. Its fixed center has all inequalities strict for n≥5. For the translated hull scaled by R=√(2(n−2)/n), the minimum support on the zero-sum unit sphere is the centered inradius. Projected coordinate, singleton upper, and pair upper constraints give clearances α=√(2/((n−1)(n−2))), β=√((n−2)/(2(n−1))), and γ=(n−4)/(2(n−2)), respectively; β>α. The strictly decreasing α and strictly increasing γ cross between 6 and 7, with no equality at integer n. Every closest outward unit constraint normal attains the minimum since the centered ball contacts that halfspace. Conversely, for any minimizing unit support direction v the point ρv of the ball is on the hull boundary; an active inequality there forces its clearance to be ρ and its unit outward normal to be v by equality in Cauchy–Schwarz. This proves exactly the listed two hole regimes. Without erasures only the coordinate and singleton bounds occur and α is the minimum.
residual_risks: The title's ‘dimension-seven’ is n=7 in the original coordinates; the zero-sum space is then six-dimensional and its sphere is S^5. The theorem body states n unambiguously.

The finite script tests the pair and negative-coordinate normals but not the positive singleton normals, despite the verification prose referring to all candidates. Their strict inequality is proved analytically. No finite random test is used to infer the theorem.

Division by R turns the h_j=1 and h_j=2 options into β and γ, with α the first term. Comparing at 6 and 7 and monotonicity yields the stated transition for every matching, regardless of its cardinality.
